title: Indicator Removal: Clear Network Connection History and Configurations
shortTitle: Indicator Removal: Clear Network Connection History and C...
summary: Clearing network connection history means deleting or rewriting the local traces left by remote access, so that a responder cannot reconstruct which hosts an intruder touched. The artefacts are scattered and platform specific. On Windows, Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) history lives in the registry under the Terminal Server Client keys as the names of previously contacted servers, in per-user Default.rdp files, and in the Terminal Server Client cache folder, while the server side records interactive logons and session events in the Security and Terminal Services logs. Linux and macOS keep comparable records in system journals, authentication logs, and remote management logs. An attacker removes registry values or whole keys, shreds the session files, or edits log files directly, and often also reverts the firewall rules, proxy settings, and remote access configuration they added, so that the host no longer looks reachable from outside. The disconnection between cause and evidence is the detection opportunity: file and registry deletion telemetry, a system journal with missing or non-sequential entries, changed file times on log files, and configuration changes with no matching change ticket all point at cleanup rather than administration. Auditing should also check whether the same account touched connection history and remote access settings in the same short window.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker erases the local records of network connections. It includes remote desktop history, saved addresses, and connection settings. The goal is to hide where they went and how they got in.
beginner.whyItMatters: Connection history is a map of an intrusion. It shows which machines a person reached and when. If that map is destroyed, you cannot see how far the attacker travelled. Old records also help you decide which machines need a full investigation.
howItWorks: Remote access tools record activity on both the machine that connects and the machine that is reached.
Windows keeps recent Remote Desktop addresses in registry keys and per-user session files.
An attacker deletes those registry values with command line tools, which leaves its own traces.
They remove or overwrite session cache files such as the per-user default remote desktop file.
On Linux and macOS they edit or delete entries in the system journal and authentication logs.
They often undo the firewall or proxy changes they made, so nothing suggests a hidden doorway.
beginner.example: Think of a taxi office that logs every trip in a book. A driver does a private job at night and then tears that page out of the book. The office sees a quiet evening, but the torn edge and the missing page number still show that something was removed.
takeaways: Clearing connection history is itself an event, so it leaves traces of the deletion.
Remote Desktop history is stored in per-user registry keys and session files, not in one place.
Configuration changes should match a change ticket, otherwise treat them as suspicious.

objectives: Explain why attackers remove network connection history and configuration data.
Identify the registry keys and files that hold Remote Desktop connection history on Windows.
Name the log sources on Linux and macOS that record remote access.
Describe how deleted or tampered log entries can be recognised during an investigation.
Explain why firewall and proxy changes are often reverted as part of this cleanup.
